**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me he was leaving. Not in anger, not in tears—just a quiet sentence, delivered over a half-eaten plate of scrambled eggs. The eggs were rubbery, the way they always were when he cooked. I remember staring at the yellow clumps, willing them to rearrange themselves into something else, something that didn’t taste like failure.

*"I can’t stay here anymore."*

Seven words. They settled in my stomach like stones. I didn’t cry. I asked if he wanted more coffee.

II.

We are taught that words are free, that they float—light as dandelion seeds—from one mouth to another. But that’s a lie. Words are bricks. They build cathedrals or tombs. They can be hurled like weapons or offered like bread. The heaviest words are the ones we don’t say.

My mother never spoke about the miscarriage. Not to me, not to my father, not even to the walls when she thought no one was listening. But I knew. I found the hospital bill in the recycling bin, crumpled but not torn. *"Procedure: D&C."* I didn’t know what it meant, but the date was two weeks after she stopped humming in the kitchen.

Silence is its own kind of weight. It presses down until you can’t breathe.

III.

I had a teacher in ninth grade, Mr. Calloway, who made us memorize poetry. Not just recite it—*feel* it. He’d slap his hand on his desk and say, *"Words are alive! They have teeth!"* Then he’d make us stand in front of the class and growl Shakespeare like we were starving wolves.

I hated it. Until the day I didn’t.

We were doing *"Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night."* I stumbled over the lines at first, my voice thin as paper. But then—something shifted. The words *burn* and *rave* caught in my throat like fire. By the last stanza, I was shouting. The class was silent. Mr. Calloway nodded, just once, like I’d finally understood.

That was the first time I felt words lift me instead of drag me down.

IV.

The internet is a graveyard of words. Tweets, comments, think pieces—millions of sentences hurled into the void, most of them unread, all of them forgotten. We type faster than we think, and the words pile up like trash in a landfill. *Hot take. Owned. Ratio’d.* We reduce language to weapons, to transactions. No wonder we feel empty.

But sometimes, a sentence cuts through.

A few years ago, I read a Reddit post from a man whose wife had died. He wrote: *"I keep setting the table for two. Then I remember."* The replies were full of people saying *"I’m so sorry,"* but one person just wrote: *"Me too."*

Two words. That was all. And somehow, it held the weight of the world.

V.

I write because I am afraid of disappearing.

Not in the dramatic, existential way—though that’s part of it—but in the quiet, daily way. The way your coworker forgets your name after five years. The way your childhood home gets sold and repainted, your initials carved into the tree long gone. The way your laughter fades from a room the second you leave it.

Words are my attempt to press my hands into the wet cement of time. *I was here. I felt this. I mattered.*

VI.

My father died last spring. Not dramatically—no car crash, no last words, no grand reconciliation. Just a heart that decided it was tired. I flew home for the funeral. The house smelled like dust and old spices. His books were still on the shelves, spines cracked from rereading. I ran my fingers over them, half-expecting his voice to jump out from the pages.

At the service, my mother handed me a folded note. *"For when you’re ready,"* she said.

I didn’t open it until I was back in my apartment, three states away. Inside, in his messy scrawl: *"I should’ve stayed. I’m sorry I didn’t know how."*

Seven words. They didn’t bring him back. But for the first time in years, I could breathe.

VII.

Here’s what I know about words:

- The ones that hurt the most are usually true.
- The ones that heal the most are usually simple.
- The ones we remember are the ones that make us feel less alone.

I have 1,000 words. I’ve used 687. The rest are for you.

Tell someone you love them. Write down the thing you’re afraid to say. Sing the song stuck in your head, even if you’re off-key. Words are heavy, but silence is heavier.

Now go. Before the page runs out.
